These results support using inductively mined rubrics as both generation guidance and reward specifications for open-ended writing.
item.dc:creator: Jihao Zhao, Shuaishuai Zu, Zhiyuan Ji, Chunlai Zhou, Biao Qin

item.title: From Documents to Spans: Span-Centric Learning for LLM-based Explainable Medical Coding
item.description: arXiv:2603.15270v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Medical coding, which assigns standardized ICD codes to clinical documents, is a fundamental yet challenging task in modern healthcare. It requires extensive knowledge of a large code space and the ability to identify and interpret sparse supporting evidence in long, noisy clinical documents. Most existing methods rely on document-level supervision, which provides limited guidance on supporting evidence and insufficient training signals for rare codes. To address these limitations, we propose Span-Centric Learning (SCL), which separates coding knowledge acquisition from its application in full documents. SCL first learns coding knowledge from short spans, then learns to use this knowledge in full documents from a small set of annotated data. Experiments show that, our approach enables an 8B LLM to surpass state-of-the-art methods using only 248 complete documents for training. It also provides explicit supporting evidence for each predicted code, with strong alignment to human annotations. Further analysis shows that the model can learn knowledge of codes absent from documents through spans and apply that knowledge to full documents.
item.dc:creator: Xu Zhang, Wenxin Ma, Chenxu Wu, Rongsheng Wang, Zhiyang He, Xiaodong Tao, Kun Zhang, S. Kevin Zhou

item.title: Explanation Generation for Contradiction Reconciliation with LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2603.22735v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Existing NLP work commonly treats contradictions as errors to be resolved by choosing which statements to accept or discard. Yet a key aspect of human reasoning in social and professional settings is the ability to hypothesize explanations that reconcile contradictions. For example, "Cassie hates coffee" and "She buys coffee everyday" appear contradictory, but are in fact compatible if Cassie was assigned the daily chore of buying coffee for all her coworkers. Despite advances in the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), their ability to hypothesize such explanations remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, we introduce the task of reconciliatory explanation generation, where models must generate explanations that effectively render contradictory statements compatible. We propose a novel method of reusing natural language inference (NLI) datasets, and introduce quality metrics that enable scalable automatic evaluation. Experiments with 13 LLMs in thinking and non-thinking modes reveal models' limited success in this task, with longer reasoning chains negatively associated with explanation success. As a proof of concept, we further adapt our introduced task and metrics for reinforcement-learning training, finding that trained models exhibit improved accuracy in non-thinking mode on two narrative reasoning benchmarks (True Detective and MuSR). Our findings highlight reconciliatory explanation generation as a challenge in LLM reasoning and motivate further work to investigate its potential for improving model capabilities.
item.dc:creator: Jason Chan, Zhixue Zhao, Robert Gaizauskas

item.title: The Necessity of Setting Temperature in LLM-as-a-Judge
item.description: arXiv:2603.28304v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated judges, yet decoding temperature is often set by intuition rather than evidence. We run over one million large scale evaluations, multiple open-source models, prompting strategies, and judging paradigms to examine how temperature affects judge reliability. Low temperatures yield consistent outputs with few errors, especially in smaller models, while higher temperatures reduce consistency and increase errors. Yet consistency alone does not guarantee sound judgments: low temperatures can narrow the range of reasoning explored. We characterize judge behavior through four reasoning personas and find that temperature shifts their distributions in model-dependent ways, most visibly in ambiguous cases where competing answers are hard to distinguish. Repeated high-temperature sampling reveals this hidden uncertainty, and combining it with majority voting or using high temperature for reasoning and low temperature for the final decision, improves agreement on ambiguous cases without hurting clear ones, at the cost of extra inference. Our findings suggest a simple rule: keep temperature low for stable outputs, but explore more when the judgment is hard.
item.dc:creator: Lujun Li, Lama Sleem, Yangjie Xu, Yewei Song, Aolin Jia, Jerome Francois, Radu State

item.title: MIXAR: Scaling Autoregressive Pixel-based Language Models to Multiple Languages and Scripts
item.description: arXiv:2604.11575v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Pixel-based language models are gaining momentum as alternatives to traditional token-based approaches, promising to circumvent tokenization challenges; however, existing models remain English-centric and are hard to train as generators. This paper introduces MIXAR, the first generative multilingual pixel-based language model, pretrained on eight high-resource languages spanning Latin and CJK scripts and scaled up to 0.5B parameters. Although pretrained on high-resource languages only, MIXAR generalizes to unseen low-resource languages better than a tokenizer-based model pretrained on the same corpus, with its largest gains on the scripts most distant from the pretraining mix, taking a step toward more equitable language technology. To make free generation work in pixel space, MIXAR replaces the notoriously unstable adversarial training stage of prior pixel-based models with a GRPO-based reinforcement-learning stage that rewards the model on its own free-running generations: it proves more stable and multiplies free-generation accuracy by up to 2.3x on multilingual benchmarks. Finally, MIXAR performs on par with comparable tokenizer-based models on discriminative benchmarks, improves consistently with scale, and withstands orthographic attacks more gracefully than tokenizer-based models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/april-tools/mixar.
item.dc:creator: Chen Hu, Yintao Tai, Antonio Vergari, Frank Keller, Alessandro Suglia

item.title: What Makes Good Instruction-Tuning Data? An In-Context Learning Perspective
item.description: arXiv:2604.25132v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Instruction-tuning datasets often contain substantial redundancy and low-quality samples, necessitating effective data selection methods. We propose an instruction data selection framework based on weighted in-context influence (wICI), which measures how effectively each candidate example reduces instruction-following difficulty for semantically related peers. Through systematic experiments, we address three key questions: what constitutes effective instruction tuning data from an in-context perspective, whether sample difficulty correlates with in-context influence, and how in-context influence translates to instruction tuning effectiveness. Experiments across multiple models and benchmarks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms existing baselines under constrained data budgets, while empirically showing that sample difficulty negatively correlates with in-context influence.
item.dc:creator: Guangzeng Han, Xiaolei Huang

item.title: Towards Emotion Consistency Analysis of Large Language Models in Emotional Conversational Contexts
item.description: arXiv:2605.06476v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we conduct an analysis to examine the consistency of Large Language Models (LLMs) with respect to their own generated responses in an emotionally-driven conversational context. Specifically, the text generated by LLM is framed as a query to the same model, and its responses are subsequently assessed. This is performed with three queries across two dimensions of extreme and moderate emotions. The three queries are, in particular, false claim queries that contain inherently wrong assumptions (false presuppositions) in increasing order of intensity. Two commercial models, Claude-3.5-haiku, GPT4o-mini, and a medium-sized model, Mistral-7B, are considered in the study. Our findings indicate that LLMs exhibit below-average performance and remain vulnerable to false beliefs embedded within queries. This susceptibility is especially pronounced for moderate emotional content. Furthermore, an extended attention-score-based analysis highlights a shift in models' priority from evaluative to generative. The results raise important considerations for LLMs' deployment in high-stakes, emotionally sensitive contexts.
item.dc:creator: Sneha Oram, Ojaswita Bhushan, Tejomay Kishor Padole, Suyash P. Awate, Pushpak Bhattacharyya

item.title: SimCT: Recovering Lost Supervision for Cross-Tokenizer On-Policy Distillation
item.description: arXiv:2605.07711v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) is a standard tool for transferring teacher behavior to a smaller student, but it implicitly assumes that teacher and student predictions are comparable token by token, an assumption that fails whenever the two models tokenize the same text differently. Under heterogeneous tokenizers, exact shared-token matching silently discards a large fraction of the teacher signal at precisely the positions where vocabularies disagree. We propose \textbf{\underline{Sim}ple \underline{C}ross-\underline{T}okenizer OPD (SimCT)}, which restores this signal by enlarging the supervision space: alongside shared tokens, SimCT compares teacher and student over short multi-token continuations that both tokenizers can realize, leaving the OPD loss form itself unchanged. We show that these units are the finest jointly tokenizable supervision interface, and that coarser alternatives remove teacher-student distinctions that are useful for on-policy learning. Across three heterogeneous teacher-student pairs on mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, SimCT shows consistent gains over shared-vocabulary OPD and representative cross-tokenizer baselines, with ablations confirming that the improvements come from recovering supervision discarded by exact shared-token matching. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}{https://github.com/sunjie279/SimCT-}.
item.dc:creator: Jie Sun, Mao Zheng, Mingyang Song, Qiyong Zhong, Yilin Cheng, Bichuan Feng, Pengfei Liu, Junfeng Fang, Xiang Wang

item.title: LLMSurgeon: Diagnosing Data Mixture of Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2605.30348v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The pretraining data mixture of Large Language Models (LLMs) constitutes their "digital DNA", shaping model behaviors, capabilities, and failure modes. Yet this composition is rarely disclosed, making post-hoc auditing of data combination or provenance difficult. In this work, we formalize Data Mixture Surgery (DMS): given only generated text from a target LLM, estimate the domain-level distribution of its pretraining corpus under a predefined taxonomy. We propose $\textbf{{LLMSurgeon}}$, a strong framework that casts DMS as an inverse problem under the label-shift assumption. Rather than directly aggregating classifier outputs, LLMSurgeon estimates a calibrated $\textit{soft}$ confusion matrix and solves a constrained inverse problem to correct systematic domain confusion and recover the latent mixture prior. To evaluate, we introduce $\textbf{{LLMScan}}$, a recipe-verifiable evaluation suite built from open-source LLMs with transparent pretraining mixtures. Across LLMScan, LLMSurgeon recovers domain mixtures with high fidelity under fixed protocols. Our work presents a practical, post-hoc approach for auditing the digital DNA of foundation models without access to their training data.
item.dc:creator: Yaxin Luo, Jiacheng Cui, Xiaohan Zhao, Xinyi Shang, Jiacheng Liu, Xinyue Bi, Zhaoyi Li, Zhiqiang Shen

item.title: Can Crowdsourcing Survive the LLM Era? A Community Survey on Human Data Collection
item.description: arXiv:2606.04924v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The widespread use of Large Language Models (LLMs) as writing tools challenges the validity of crowdsourced data, as crowdworkers may outsource tasks to models. To better understand how this is addressed, we surveyed 155 researchers in NLP and related disciplines about their experiences and opinions on collecting free-text responses via crowdsourcing. This paper provides an overview of practitioners' challenges, mitigation strategies, and the foreseen implications on data quality. 44% of respondents reported observing LLM usage in their crowdsourced data. While 93% of them had anticipated this, half were unsure what precautions to take. The most prevalent detection strategies are distinctive textual style patterns and unusually fast completion times. Overall, survey responses show that the research community is aware of the problem and taking measures, but existing efforts remain insufficient to fully address it. Finally, we derive a set of considerations to guide future crowdsourced free-text data collection in the era of LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Aswathy Velutharambath, Neele Falk, Sofie Labat, Tarun Tater, Amelie Wuehrl

item.title: Is Text All You Need? Text as a Universal Information Bottleneck for Speech LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2606.09366v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) provide a powerful reasoning backbone for speech understanding, but integrating continuous acoustic signals into a pretrained LLM remains challenging. A central design question is how to tie speech representations to the LLM's text input space while preserving the continuous variation needed for different speech tasks. In this work, we propose Convex Gate (C-Gate), a speech-LLM bridge that represents each frame as a convex combination of frozen token embeddings. This architectural convex-hull constraint fixes the output codebook while allowing continuous mixtures learned from task supervision. With a Whisper-large-v3 encoder, a partially adapted Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct decoder, and joint training on speech recognition, emotion recognition, and spoken reasoning, C-Gate performs accurate transcription and emotion recognition, our representative semantic and acoustic tasks, through one shared decoder. On text-only benchmarks, the adapted decoder loses instruction-following and MMLU accuracy and matches or exceeds the original model on GSM8K and HellaSwag. We further design analyses and interventions on the trained model to examine where the bridge sequence carries task information and how the decoder reads it. These findings show how fixed text embeddings can support both semantic and acoustic readouts through continuous speech-conditioned mixtures.
item.dc:creator: Ming-Hao Hsu, Yuxuan Hu, Shujie Liu, Jinyu Li, Yan Lu, Zhizheng Wu

item.title: Reasoning without Gold Standards: A Proxy-Judge Theory of Autoformalization
item.description: arXiv:2606.09449v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Autoformalization (AF) requires both prover acceptance and fidelity to an informal source, but prover acceptance alone cannot establish fidelity, and expert-validated reference formalizations are costly to obtain. We introduce a reference-free proxy-judge framework, which separates correctness into grounding, statement faithfulness, coverage, and inference, and a theory of how imperfect checks shape iterative refinement. We establish three results. First, for a fixed sequence of candidates, an added proxy's false-positive and false-negative rates bound its effect on the pass-but-wrong rate. Second, damage to a correct formalization requires a false rejection that exposes it to further refinement, and harmful revisions are then retained through unguarded changes, missed changes, or prover progress that overrides judge warnings. Third, a decomposition of the final pass rate distinguishes continued refinement, generation of new candidates, and their success in passing the checks. We instantiate the framework with eight proxies and test these predictions on ProofNet and miniF2F in Lean~4 and on e-SNLI and ProntoQA in Isabelle/HOL. Under single-proxy removal, no prediction written before the runs is contradicted, and all traced breaks follow the identified failure routes. The results connect proxy reliability to the benefits, risks, and limits of refinement without reference formalizations.
item.dc:creator: Lei Xu, Xin Quan, Andr\'e Freitas

item.title: LLMs Infer Cultural Context but Fail to Apply It When Responding
item.description: arXiv:2606.17688v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent work has shown that LLMs overrepresent dominant cultures, particularly Western ones, while marginalizing others. We investigate whether this affects models' ability to generate culturally adapted responses by evaluating their use of local measurement units based on the user's perceived cultural background. We introduce Cultural and Pragmatic Response Inference (CAPRI), a dataset of conversations with varying levels of cultural cues. Experiments with state-of-the-art LLMs show that models can infer cultural background and recall relevant conventions, but often fail to utilize the information to adapt their answers to the relevant cultural conventions, unless explicitly prompted to perform the tasks sequentially. We further evaluate adaptation to the interpretation of time and quantity expressions, two subjective language grounding dimensions that are affected by culture. We find that models increasingly adapt their answers as cultural cues accumulate, but their priors are not culture-neutral, sometimes aligning with the model's country of origin. Overall, CAPRI provides a resource for future research aimed at narrowing the gap between cultural knowledge and culturally adaptive language generation.
item.dc:creator: Yisong Miao, Jian Zhu, Vered Shwartz

item.title: Learning at the Right Pace: Adaptive Data Scheduling Improves LLM Reinforcement Learning
item.description: arXiv:2606.22305v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve remarkable reasoning capabilities through reinforcement learning (RL) post-training. However, existing RL post-training commonly relies on uniform data sampling, which ignores the semantic structure of the training data and the evolving capability of the training policy. To address these limitations, we propose Adaptive Data Scheduling (ADS), a dual-level data scheduling framework that combines adaptive sampling across semantic clusters with policy-boundary sample selection. At the cluster level, ADS organizes samples according to semantic patterns and adapts the inter-cluster sampling distribution to prioritize clusters within the policy's current reach. At the sample level, ADS tracks prompts near the policy's capability boundary within each cluster to obtain informative relative advantages. Experimental results across three LLMs and seven reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that ADS improves average accuracy by 5.5% over Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). Notably, ADS consistently improves RL methods with different objective designs, highlighting its potential as a general data scheduling strategy. The source code is available at: https://github.com/Richard-zrx/ADS.
item.dc:creator: Zicheng Xu, Ruixuan Zhang, Yu-Neng Chuang, Xiuyi Lou, Hoang Anh Duy Le, Oren Gal, Alexander S. Szalay, Zhaozhuo Xu, Guanchu Wang, Vladimir Braverman

item.title: Hitting a Moving Target: Test-Time Adaptation for AI Text Detection under Continual Distribution Shift
item.description: arXiv:2606.25152v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Deployed AI text detection approaches are supervised, relying on training-time access to labeled datasets of both human-written and AI-generated text. This approach is vulnerable to three types of distribution shifts that occur continually post-deployment, and for which labeled data is often unavailable: adversarial humanization, new LLMs being released, and unidentifiable temporal drift in human writing after widespread LLM usage. Simultaneously, existing approaches do not leverage a key signal of LLM usage: inference-time homogeneity. We propose a test-time adaptation (TTA) approach that adapts to distribution shifts by leveraging homogeneity among unlabeled samples observed at inference time. Empirically, we find that state-of-the-art supervised detectors systematically fail when they encounter distribution shifts in AI-generated and human writing, both adversarial and natural, while TTA with semi-supervised learning is largely robust; e.g., the commercial model Pangram detects just 27.0% of our adversarial AI-generated text, compared to 93.3% for our test-time approach. We establish that TTA is a promising framework for AI text detection in the wild.
item.dc:creator: Kevin Ren, Manish Raghavan, Nikhil Garg

item.title: From Signals to Transfer: A Factorised Study of Probe-Based Uncertainty Estimation in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2606.27679v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Probe-based uncertainty estimation (UE) has emerged as a prominent approach to detect hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning uncertainty from internal model signals. Yet, recent methods vary simultaneously across feature design, training data construction, and evaluation setting, obscuring what actually drives performance. To address this issue, we propose a factorised study of probe-based UE under matched conditions. Our results show that raw hidden states and attention features are difficult to outperform in-domain. However, under distribution shift, structured and compressed features are more robust, suggesting that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to measure progress. Furthermore, prompting and label construction significantly affect probe behaviour. Building on these empirical design principles, we construct benchmark-pretrained probes that retain useful discriminative signal on open-ended factual generation. Their competitive performance relative to limited-label target setting probes and sampling-based estimators suggests that they can provide a practical starting point for subsequent target-domain adaptation. More broadly, our work encourages deployment-oriented evaluation of probe-based uncertainty estimators.
item.dc:creator: Ponhvoan Srey, Xiaobao Wu, Cong-Duy Nguyen, Quang Minh Nguyen, Duc Anh Vu, Anh Tuan Luu

item.title: Right Answer, Wrong Tokens: Tail-Aware Credit Calibration for RLVR
item.description: arXiv:2607.07976v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Although reinforcement learning (RL) improves the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs), GRPO-style methods can suffer from a positive-credit contamination failure mode. Specifically, uniform credit assignment can reinforce locally erroneous tail tokens alongside useful tokens within successful trajectories. To address this problem, we propose Tail-Aware Credit calibratiOn (TACO), which calibrates the positive credit assigned to such tokens without token-level error labels. To this end, TACO lets the policy serve as its own reference, assessing each sampled token's rarity relative to the policy's local expectations to compute a tail-risk score. Using this score as a proxy for potential local errors, TACO softly reduces positive credit for high tail-risk tokens while retaining nonzero weights, limiting their reinforcement without eliminating opportunities to learn useful rare patterns. Experiments across four LLMs and eight reasoning benchmarks show that TACO consistently improves over GRPO-style baselines. Notably, TACO also improves training stability, supporting sustained performance gains in long-horizon RL. The source code is available at: https://github.com/xiuyilou/TACO.
item.dc:creator: Xiuyi Lou, Zicheng Xu, Yu-Neng Chuang, Hoang Anh Duy Le, Zhaozhuo Xu, Guanchu Wang, Vladimir Braverman

item.title: X-Alpha: An AI Quant Researcher with Memory-Driven Self-Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2607.08332v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Human quantitative researchers mine alpha through an iterative process: they derive hypotheses from financial knowledge, implement and test them as factors, and use the resulting evidence to guide subsequent research. Yet automated alpha mining faces three key bottlenecks: noisy financial knowledge is not directly actionable, exploration can remain confined to similar mechanisms, and feedback may remain tied to individual mining runs. To address these bottlenecks, we introduce X-Alpha, an AI Quant Researcher that couples persistent research memory with continuous hypothesis-to-code discovery. Report-to-Memory Abstraction (RMA) uses a multi-layer filtering-and-abstraction process to convert financial reports into actionable, data-compatible research paths. Memory-driven routing uses accumulated experience to redirect exploration and define a targeted search space for each cycle. Within each cycle, hypotheses are implemented as executable factors and refined through empirical validation and code-based evolution. Empirical outcomes are consolidated into persistent research memory to guide subsequent exploration, enabling memory-driven self-evolution across cycles. We evaluate X-Alpha on five equity indices spanning mainland China, the United States, and Hong Kong, with comprehensive experiments centered on CSI300. Experiments show strong alpha discovery performance against baselines, with improvements in factor quality and signal diversity and consistent generation-level gains across multiple markets and prediction horizons.
item.dc:creator: Fengyuan Liu, Yuchen Fu, Yuqi Wang, Fengyuan Liu, Mukai Li, Qi Liu

item.title: Amplitude-Only FFN Intervention for Tool-Structured LLM Inference: Method, Gated Evaluation Protocol, and Cross-Model Empirical Results
item.description: arXiv:2607.11183v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study Amplitude Gating (AG), an inference-time intervention that masks feed-forward network (FFN) activation coordinates while keeping pretrained weights fixed. Six SwiGLU sites separate shared and gate-only inputs, expanded gate/value channels, and the FFN output. Magnitude-ranked entropy masks and a Newton-Schulz windowed ranking variant provide alternative forward paths without retraining. The corrected September collection covers three Qwen checkpoints and eight text/tool endpoints. Under frozen local text scorers, the displayed Qwen3.5-9B non-NS configurations improve two function-call endpoints by +2.61 and +2.67 percentage points (pp), and static ToolBench in/out-domain endpoints by +1.64 and +2.82 pp. Comparing the lower historical/September AG mean with the higher baseline mean leaves positive margins on these routes. This supports robustness to the two observed executions, rather than formal statistical significance. JSON gains are small and displayed L-Eval effects are negative. These endpoints measure lexical or answer/action-name agreement rather than executed-tool success. Protocol-specific offline selector and Per-Sample Fix-Harm Evaluation (PFHE) analyses complement the fixed-route results. Current experimental data do not establish a significant random-forest (RF) benefit; further experiments are needed. AG provides a task-dependent intervention surface, with causal mechanisms, equal-budget advantages, repeated-run uncertainty, and serving cost still open.
item.dc:creator: Sheng Xu, Zhen Chen, Junhua Wang, Boyuan Huang, Ke Jia, Jiadun Zhu, Yiming Xu

item.title: Reasoning Error from Known Fact: Step-Level Self-Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization for LLMs
item.description: arXiv:2607.18915v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: With the rapid advancement of large language models (LLMs), modern systems not only possess strong foundational capabilities and extensive knowledge, but can also solve complex problems via long, multi-step reasoning. However, as reasoning traces become longer, LLMs may produce a substantial amount of hallucinated content during the reasoning process, which is often difficult to detect. In this work, we conduct a fine-grained analysis of hallucinations arising in LLM reasoning and find that the reasoning traces are particularly prone to Context-Sensitive Factual Hallucinations: cases where the model actually has the relevant knowledge, yet makes factual errors due to contextual interference during reasoning. To address this issue, we propose Step-level Self-Consistency Group Relative Policy Optimization (SSC-GRPO), which assigns step-level rewards to reasoning traces by computing self-consistency scores of individual steps across multiple rollouts. Compared with prior methods, SSC-GRPO achieves state-of-the-art performance on both mathematical reasoning benchmarks and hallucination leaderboards. Our results offer a new perspective for detecting and mitigating hallucinations in the reasoning process of large language models.
item.dc:creator: Xiaomeng Hu, Jiaqi Hu, Hao Chen, Qi Zhang, Zhanming Shen, Wentao Ye, Junbo Zhao

item.title: Beyond Relevance-Centric Retrieval: Rubric-Oriented Document Set Selection and Ranking
item.description: arXiv:2607.19747v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As large language models and AI agents become the primary consumers of search results, document set quality determines the upper bound of downstream generation. Yet existing evaluation systems remain confined to scoring documents independently and aggregating via nDCG, ignoring inter-document interactions (redundancy, conflict, complementarity) and unable to answer what makes one document set better than another. To address these issues, we propose a complete evaluate-diagnose-optimize framework. We design SetwiseEvalKit, a three-level, nine-dimension document set evaluation benchmark covering both short-form and long-form scenarios, comprising approximately 28K high-quality evaluation rubrics. We systematically evaluate 12 rerankers: even the best method achieves no more than 45% coverage, cross-document coordination dimensions are universally weak, and no single method maintains top performance across both settings. Building on this, we propose Rubric4Setwise, a training-free method that converts rubric-based evaluation criteria into document set selection signals, achieving the best downstream generation performance with fewer documents and search rounds. It is the only method that maintains state-of-the-art results across both scenarios, validating the effectiveness of closing the loop from evaluation to optimization.
item.dc:creator: Kailin Jiang, Lei Liu, Jian Xi, Hui Xu, Junlin Liu, Baochen Fu, Bin Li, Vichwang, Yu Lu, Haibo Shi

item.title: M$^3$R-Bench: A Unified Benchmark for Evidence-Grounded Multimodal Metaphor Understanding
item.description: arXiv:2608.05817v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multimodal metaphor understanding requires identifying cross-domain Target-Source mappings and inferring sentiment from visual and textual evidence. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate these subtasks separately and lack evidence-grounded explanations, limiting their ability to assess coherent cross-modal reasoning. To enable unified and evidence-grounded evaluation, we introduce M$^3$R-Bench, a benchmark of 1,000 human-annotated image-text instances with joint labels for metaphor occurrence, Target-Source mapping, and sentiment, alongside stage-wise explanations for evidence identification, mapping establishment, and sentiment inference. Evaluations reveal that existing models frequently rely on textual shortcuts and produce Target-Source mappings inconsistent with visual evidence. To address this evidence-mapping mismatch, we propose M$^3$R-Reasoner, which combines curriculum-based reasoning supervision with task-aware reinforcement learning. Built on an 8B-parameter backbone, M$^3$R-Reasoner achieves 37.90% Joint Label Accuracy (JLA) metric, outperforming the strongest proprietary baseline by 19.50 percentage points. It further surpasses GPT-5.5 in image-text evidence and sentiment justification scores by 28.45 and 28.11 points, respectively. The dataset and code are available at https://github.com/hongshi4/m3r-bench-artifact.
item.dc:creator: Hong Jiang, Junnan Zhu, Jingwang Huang, Xiao Sun, Yuming Yang, Jiang Zhong, Ruirui Chen, Jingman Shi, Hao Wu, Nayu Liu, Xinyi Jiang, Kaiwen Wei

item.title: Archer: Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback in Diffusion Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2608.08086v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) can revise earlier predictions as context evolves, but rollback requires costly full-sequence recomputation. Conventional key-value (KV) caching assumes immutable historical states and is difficult to reconcile with such revision. We introduce Adaptive Reuse of Cached Hidden States for Efficient Rollback (Archer), a training-free caching method for rollback-capable DLMs. Archer recomputes the mutable response at every update while reusing prompt K/V within a bounded response-state neighborhood. This asymmetric boundary amortizes prompt computation without restricting rollback. Bounded reuse also delays feedback from tentative tokens while keeping response revision active. Our analysis characterizes the cache boundary, bounds state-dependent approximation error, and gives a decoder-margin condition for preserving full-refresh decisions. On code-generation benchmarks, Archer achieves the best mean performance of 33.63% with a 2.57x mean speedup, reaching 2.95x speedup on a single benchmark. On non-code benchmarks, Archer achieves up to 4.33x speedup over LLaDA-Confidence while improving average accuracy. Controlled analyses support the delayed prompt feedback mechanism. Our code is available at https://github.com/Hxnng/Archer
item.dc:creator: Xuning He, Qingyuan Shi, Zinan Sheng, Yongding Tao, Huanyu Liu, Ge Li, Xue Jiang, Yihong Dong

item.title: Closed-Loop Molecular Inverse Design with Semantic LLM Surrogates
item.description: arXiv:2608.22967v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Practical molecular inverse design is rarely a one-shot generation problem; it often involves enriching a pool of molecules that match a desired property profile under a limited oracle budget. Bayesian optimization (BO) offers a natural framework for this setting, with standard Gaussian-process (GP) surrogates operating in continuous embedding spaces. We propose LoopMol, a closed-loop framework whose large language model (LLM) surrogate reasons directly over task instructions, SMILES-level optimization histories, and oracle feedback. At each iteration, the surrogate selects informative reference molecules under an exploration--exploitation principle, optionally with a concise guidance sentence. These outputs condition the next generation round and yield an inspectable optimization trace. Experiments on six drug and material tasks across three Llamole backbones show that the LLM-based variant improves over one-shot generation and is competitive with or stronger than GP-based BO. They also reveal a domain-dependent interface: reference-only conditioning performs better on binary drug tasks, while adding a concise guidance sentence generally benefits continuous material tasks.
item.dc:creator: Yaoyao Xu, Xinjian Zhao, Xiaozhuang Song, Lei Bai, Tianshu Yu

item.title: DataKernelBench: Can LLMs Optimize Database Queries on GPUs?
item.description: arXiv:2608.25061v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: GPUs increasingly accelerate database systems, but query-specific peak performance still often relies on hand-written kernels. Existing LLM kernel benchmarks focus on machine learning operators, leaving irregular, heterogeneous, data-movement-heavy database-style operators untested. We introduce DataKernelBench, which translates SQL into validated PyTorch TorchPlan programs and evaluates LLMs that optimize either the core tensor-bounded snippet or the full query in CUDA or Triton through execution-guided repair. Across ten proprietary and open-weight models on TPC-H SF10 with an H100 GPU, the strongest full-query CUDA configuration achieves $2.11\times$ speedup over the TorchPlan baseline at full pass rate. We find that higher-performing implementations commonly use kernel fusion and execution-strategy changes, stronger models benefit most from full-query specialization, and workload context matters more than hardware context. To handle data larger than GPU memory, we extend TorchPlan with Dask-cuDF for on-demand partition loading on TPC-H SF100 with four H100 GPUs, achieving $2.54\times$ speedup. Project page: https://kerneldf.github.io/datakernelbench
item.dc:creator: Gokul Karthik Kumar, Yotam Perlitz, Corey Lammie, Andrea Giovannini, Katja Hose

item.title: Language Models Can Control Their Own Attention
item.description: arXiv:2609.02737v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Language models spend most of their attention on a small fraction of context, yet they read the entire KV cache to find the few tokens that matter. If the user asks about a previous detail in a 1M-token conversation, global attention layers must scan the full context to generate each token of the reply. A prominent approach pre-selects relevant tokens via lightweight proxy scores, but this extrinsic scoring still incurs O(N) per step. We take an intrinsic approach motivated by the simple question: wouldn't the model already know which parts of the context are relevant? We introduce Declarative Attention (DA), a protocol that elicits the model to declare where it needs to attend within its chain-of-thought, partitioning generation into three modes: <global> (full context), <focus> (a specific region), and <local> (recent output only). The inference engine parses these declarations like tool calls and skips most of the KV cache read. Under zero-shot evaluation across 15 long-context tasks, DA on off-the-shelf models (Gemma-4-31B, Qwen-3.6-27B) reduces total attended tokens per response (45.8%, 19.6%), despite extra decoding steps, with modest accuracy drops (1.40pp, 2.10pp) that shrink with model scale. DA unlocks a new axis of sparse attention, with further potential under training-based methods. Code is available at https://github.com/itsnamgyu/declarative-attention.
item.dc:creator: Namgyu Ho, Huzama Ahmad, Woosung Koh, Se-Young Yun, Tal Schuster, Cicero Nogueira dos Santos

item.title: RefactorPlatform: An Open-Source Harness for Controlled Evaluation of Repository-Scale Refactoring Agents
item.description: arXiv:2609.04898v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Repository-scale refactoring requires coding agents to propagate a single change across many interdependent files without altering program behavior, yet to our knowledge no existing harness isolates the design choices that determine agent success on this task. We present RefactorPlatform, an open-source evaluation harness that holds the environment fixed and varies each design axis explicitly: model backbone (via OpenRouter and GitHub Copilot CLI), execution regime (baseline, retrieval-augmented, and multi-agent), and prompt specificity. Each run executes in an isolated workspace with live terminal streaming, per-task logging of tokens, diffs, and transcripts, AST-based verification, and exportable telemetry for audit and reproduction. Demonstrating the platform on 100 multi-file RefactorBench tasks across four model families, we illustrate the analyses it supports: AST-aware chunking outperforms naive token-window chunking by 25-30 percentage points (pp) across prompt modes, whereas naive retrieval falls below the retrieval-free baseline; a lean retrieval-augmented single agent (86%) beats the sub-agent configuration we evaluated (66%) on matched tasks with no task passing under delegation that fails under retrieval; and retrieval's accuracy gains absorb its token overhead, leaving cost per successful refactoring unchanged. RefactorPlatform is open-sourced to make refactoring-agent evaluation reproducible and auditable.
item.dc:creator: Aziz Ben Amor, Drish Mali, Mann Acharya, Vijayasri Iyer, S\'ebastien Brati\`eres

item.title: NeoHorse-1: Towards Recursive Self-Improvement via Agentic Post-Training with Routing Harness
item.description: arXiv:2609.08183v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recursive self-improvement (RSI) requires a concrete mechanism through which an AI system observes its capabilities and converts that evidence into the next round of learning. We present NeoHorse-1, a family of agent-native models developed to explore this path through agentic post-training. Our system combines a heterogeneous model pool with intelligent routing, recording the predicted capability demand, selected service tier, and subsequent interaction for each user turn. These records are converted into training examples that preserve interleaved reasoning, tool calls, and harness context, and are admitted through structural validation, six-dimensional semantic evaluation, and subscene-level labeling. Routing signals organize supervised fine-tuning into a three-stage curriculum and extend to routing-guided on-policy distillation, where a teacher supervises student-generated responses under the same progression. Capability-guided allocation then converts evaluation feedback into the next training mixture, closing an evaluation-selection-update loop in which what the system learns to do shapes what it learns from next. Across eleven benchmarks covering harness-based agents, tool use, coding, and instruction following, post-training raises the macro-average from 58.94 to 64.87 at 4B and from 65.60 to 69.04 at 9B, substantially narrowing the aggregate gap between the post-trained 4B model and the 9B base model. We further adapt NeoHorse-1-4B into NeoHorse-Jev-4B, a prefill-only model that returns structured decisions and probabilities for agent workflows. NeoHorse-1 provides an initial prototype of this feedback-driven process and a path toward harness-mediated RSI across successive iterations.
item.dc:creator: NeoHorse Team, Guoliang Cao, Guohao Dai, Tianyu Guo, Kai Han, Hailin Hu, Zihan Jiang, Xiang Kuang, Boxun Li, Yulong Li, Zehua Pei, Yuchuan Tian, Jiamin Wang, Yu Wang, Yunhe Wang, Yihong Wu, Haiyang Xu, Shuo Zhang, Hang Zhou, Siyang Cheng, Jiayu Fan, Wei He, Qingrui Jiao, Hongguang Li, Zhiyuan Li, Runke Liu, Xi Liu, Xinchen Liu, Sinno Jialin Pan, Yi Ren, Liuyang Song, Chenyu Wang, Bei Yu, Quanlu Zhang, Xiangyu Zhang, Mengyu Zheng, Yingjie Zong

item.title: $\Phi$-Bench: Can Large Language Models Engineer the Infrastructure That Powers Them?
item.description: arXiv:2609.10226v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now show strong reasoning and coding abilities, raising the prospect that they could assist in developing and optimizing the very infrastructure that powers them. Existing benchmarks, however, mainly focus on isolated kernels, predefined operators, or pre-specified optimization targets, and cannot evaluate open-ended, long-horizon LLM infrastructure engineering. To address this gap, we present $\Phi$-Bench, a benchmark of 85 tasks grounded in real LLM training and inference codebases. The tasks cover nine categories of LLM infrastructure and come in three formats, ranging from kernel function completion to long-horizon implementation and repository-wide end-to-end optimization. They are built by a construction pipeline that turns real pull requests, issues, and repository code into executable tasks with validated tests, and every reward is gated by correctness and anti-hacking checks. Across eight frontier models, the strongest model, Claude Opus 5, scores only 36.53%, and every model performs worse on long-horizon, repository-level implementation than on kernel-level tasks. Trajectory analysis further suggests that stronger models treat optimization as controlled experimentation, validating ideas with cheap local runs and ruling out confounders before drawing conclusions. We will open-source $\Phi$-Bench to facilitate future research on LLM agents' ability to develop and optimize the LLM infrastructure that powers themselves.
item.dc:creator: Leilei Ding, Shumin Wang, Yuting Huang, Fanqi Wan, Yinmin Zhang, Qi Han, Yiming Xu, Feiyuan Zhang, Xiaomeng Chu, Guoliang You, Wuyang Zhang, Daxin Jiang, Yanyong Zhang

item.title: A primer on evaluation methods for large language models in healthcare
item.description: arXiv:2609.14819v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have a growing range of applications in medicine, and their evaluation is critical for ensuring they provide benefit and not harm. This evaluation can be more challenging than traditional machine learning for many reasons, including probabilistic and open-ended outputs, and behavior that shifts with prompt design and accumulated context. This review covers four key areas of LLM evaluation: principles of study design, statistical methods, capability evaluation and clinical application evaluation. Capability evaluation considers different benchmarks, including multiple-choice, agentic and multi-turn benchmarks, alongside operational metrics like token usage and latency. Clinical application evaluation addresses establishing accuracy of free text outputs, such as human review and LLM-as-a-judge, and clinical trial approaches. Across sections, we describe underlying concepts and potential pitfalls, while emphasizing the importance of aligning evaluation methods with the research question. Together, this article aims to provide a pragmatic basis for designing and executing rigorous evaluations of healthcare LLMs.
item.dc:creator: Suzannah E McKinney, Phuc Vu, Samuel A Justice, Christopher Humphries, Alyssa Pradhan, Timothy J Keyes, Kameron C Black, John L Havlik, David JH Wu, Jack W O'Sullivan, Ethan Goh, Sarah F Mercaldo, James M Hillis

item.title: DischargeBench: Pre-Deployment Evaluation of LLM Discharge Educators through Persona-Grounded Patient Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2609.20827v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Effective discharge education is personalized: a clinician adapts the discharge plan to each patient's literacy, recall, and personality. Before large language models (LLMs) take on this role with real patients, they need to be evaluated in conversations with diverse patients, yet existing evaluations target static, artifact-generation, or question-answering tasks. We introduce **DischargeBench**, a pre-deployment benchmark in which a candidate LLM educator teaches a persona-grounded simulated patient in an open-ended, multi-turn conversation. We curate **MIMIC-IV-Ext-DischargeBench**, 320 cases across 16 ICD chapters, each paired with a patient persona that varies personality, education level, health literacy, and recall. Each conversation is scored on Conversation Quality, Topic Checklist Score (TCS), Simulated Comprehension Score (SCS), and a Claim-Level Safety Audit (CLSA) by an LLM judge validated against physician annotations. Across eight closed- and open-source LLMs, the best model scored only 0.70 on TCS and 0.72 on SCS, and distrustful and anxious patients lowered comprehension for every model. DischargeBench is intended as a screening step before human evaluation, not as evidence of readiness to educate patients.
item.dc:creator: Won Seok Jang, Youngbin Jang, Chanyoung Ko, Hyunwook Kim, Zonghai Yao, Hong Yu

item.title: One Reference or Many? Rethinking Multi-Reference Training for Intermediate-Entropy Text Generation
item.description: arXiv:2609.22805v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Natural language generation (NLG) ranges from highly constrained tasks, such as machine translation, to open-ended tasks like dialogue generation. Between them lie peer-review generation and image captioning, where one input admits several valid, overlapping outputs. We measure this intermediary region with Von Neumann entropy ($\hat{H}\approx0.6$ vs. 0.15 translation, 0.92 dialogue). Single-reference training discards valid perspectives, while multi-reference training introduces high-variance, unaligned targets. To tackle this, we propose target-side consolidation, that is, merging all references for an input into a single target which preserves every distinct information unit. To this end, we introduce MERC-67K, pairing 36,537 papers and 31,014 images with their original and consolidated references. In human evaluation, models trained using consolidated reviews obtain an average rank of 1.70 (out of 4) for coverage against 2.51-2.98 for baselines, and win 63.5-74.0% of pairwise comparisons. Models trained using consolidated captions obtain an average rank of 1.87 for overall caption quality (accuracy and naturalness) against 2.64-2.82 for baselines and obtain the highest reference-free LongCLIPScore (0.839 vs best baseline's 0.816). For reviews, multi-reference training often under-performs zero-shot inference, and consolidation's gains over multi-reference training hold across Llama3.1, Mistralv0.3, and Qwen2.5. Consolidation uses $\sim$4$\times$ (reviews) and 5$\times$ (captions) fewer individual references during optimization. Dataset and code will be released upon acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Maitreya Prafulla Chitale, Ketaki Mangesh Shetye, Yash More, Harshit Gupta, Manav Chaudhary, Manish Shrivastava, Vasudeva Varma

item.title: Jev for Scientific Decisions: Evaluating Semantic Choices and Their Consequences
item.description: arXiv:2609.24965v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scientific workflows often require choosing among known relations before a deterministic calculation can proceed. Whether observations share a culture, treatment or reference standard can change the scientific meaning of the resulting count or comparison. We evaluate Jev as a semantic decision component using a harness that follows its documented guidance and assigns arithmetic to code. The study compares twelve model configurations on twenty source-grounded Choices across ten scientific cases, each repeated five times. We measure semantic selections, downstream outputs and final claim labels separately. Jev matched five other configurations at complete semantic correctness and achieved the lowest observed median latency among successful responses. Across three comparison models, seven wrong selections on one culture-history question changed downstream counts while preserving the correct final label. These results identify a useful role for Jev in prepared scientific decision tasks and show why evaluating that role requires checking the relations and quantities that a workflow will reuse.
item.dc:creator: Boyuan Deng, Shuyi Fan, Hongyang Zhang, Xinhong Xie

item.title: Brain-to-Language Decoding: Tasks, Signals, Methods, Evaluation, Practical Use and Beyond
item.description: arXiv:2609.27650v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Brain-to-language decoding translates neural activity associated with language production, internal speech and perception into linguistic or expressive outputs. It offers a route to restoring communication after speech loss and a means of studying how the brain represents language. Advances in neural recording and representation learning have expanded the field from constrained recognition and acoustic reconstruction to text generation, streaming personalised speech and facial animation. This survey synthesises these developments across invasive and non-invasive measurements, drawing on a search without a lower year limit and source-led updates through September 2026. We connect Articulated, Inner and Perceived tasks to the neural populations they engage, the representations available to decoders and the outputs those representations can support. We examine model development, public resources and the evolution of evaluation, and compare published performance and communication costs within their reported protocols. The synthesis identifies complementary routes to progress: phonetic, acoustic and semantic targets preserve different aspects of a message; shared representations support reuse across recording conditions and tasks; and online communication increasingly depends on calibration, feedback and user control alongside decoding accuracy. Shared benchmarks enable algorithmic comparisons, while longitudinal studies reveal the demands of sustained use. We discuss these developments and their remaining limitations, then outline a prospective five-level trajectory from commands and language to meaning, scenarios and bidirectional cognitive exchange
item.dc:creator: Yiqian Yang, Yiqun Duan, Chenyu Liu, Yiqi Wang, Xinliang Zhou, Chin-Teng Lin, Yu Zhang

item.title: GSM: Efficient Language Modeling with Shared Global State
item.description: arXiv:2609.33465v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Improving language model efficiency requires not only cheaper operations but also eliminating redundant computation. We argue that effective modeling requires information accessibility and computational depth, but not repeated historical retrieval across layers. Guided by this principle, we introduce the Global State Model (GSM), a causal encoder--decoder architecture that separates historical information acquisition from deep computation. The encoder progressively aggregates long-range information through multi-stage sparse retrieval into a fixed-size shared state, while decoder layers perform successive transformations over this state without repeated historical access. This design makes decoder attention and cache costs independent of history length, while dependency-aware pruning further reduces prefill computation. Experiments across multiple model scales show that GSM achieves downstream performance comparable to matched DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-based baselines, with improvements at some scales, while preserving long-context retrieval capabilities. GSM also improves training and inference throughput and reduces cache overhead. These results demonstrate that eliminating architectural redundancy offers an effective path toward efficient language modeling without sacrificing information accessibility or computational depth.
item.dc:creator: Yunao Zheng, Bin Wen, Xiaojie Wang, Kaiyu Jiang, Xuanyu Zheng, Changyi Liu, Hongyi Fu, Jianxiong Wang, Tianke Zhang, Haonan Fan, Yingxin Li, Jiankang Chen, Xu Wang, Tingting Gao, Han Li

item.title: LEAP: Learned Block-wise Evidence Retrieval for Long Audio-Video Perception
item.description: arXiv:2609.39938v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Hour-scale audio-visual question answering is constrained by a context dilemma: dense whole-recording encoding rapidly exhausts context limits, whereas uniform temporal compression severely dilutes fine-grained acoustic and visual evidence. We introduce LEAP, a framework where the model retrieves its own evidence without placing the whole recording in one context. LEAP divides a recording into fixed-duration blocks, applying a lightweight localization pass to each block to score short candidate windows. The highest-ranked windows are pooled and re-encoded in a single bounded answer pass. Consequently, the answer input and peak context remain independent of the recording duration. By decoupling evidence localization from reasoning, our framework can localize candidate temporal windows over pre-computed transcripts without decoding media frames, while preserving fine-grained visual and non-speech evidence by routing the final answering pass over raw audio-visual streams. LEAP trains both stages: a localization LoRA improves the selected windows, and an answer LoRA improves the answers read from the same windows. The block grid natively supports causal queries, enabling LEAP to support streaming inference without streaming-specific training. Across several AVQA benchmarks, LEAP improves over the Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B baseline by 4.5-16.8%, and transfers to a second omni-modal backbone, MiniCPM-o 4.5, surpassing its published results by 3.1-13.0%.
item.dc:creator: Juyi Lin, Zhiqiang Lao, Jiali Cui, Lin Zhao, Pu Zhao, Dichang Zhang, Arman Akbari, Yu Qi, Xinru Jiang, Yanzhi Wang, Heather Yu, Liang Peng

item.title: A generative-informed neuro-symbolic framework for syntactic ambiguity resolution: Evidence from Arabic DPs
item.description: arXiv:2610.02529v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Syntactic ambiguity poses a persistent challenge for Arabic NLP, particularly in morphologically rich nominal constructions where multiple structu6ral interpretations may be compatible with the same surface sequence. This study proposes a generatively informed neuro-symbolic framework for resolving structural ambiguity in Modern Standard Arabic (MSA) DPs. The framework integrates generative syntactic notions with AraBERT by representing ambiguity as a candidate-based decision task in which linguistically motivated alternatives are explicitly constructed and evaluated through candidate-conditioned input representations. Findings indicate that the model achieved 96.88% accuracy, 95.92% macro-F1, 96.83% weighted F1, and 93.94% binary F1 on the unseen evaluation set. Class-level analysis revealed asymmetric performance, with recall of 99.71% for High/VP Attachment (N1) and 89.26% for Low/NP/Embedded Attachment (N2), indicating greater difficulty in recovering the embedded interpretation. The study concludes that formal syntactic representations can be operationalized within Transformer-based NLP as an explicit interface between linguistic structure and contextual neural modeling, providing a controlled and interpretable approach to Arabic syntactic ambiguity resolution and beyond.
item.dc:creator: Mohammed Damom, Mohammed Q. Shormani, Muneef Y. Alshawsh, Ashraf A. Naji, Mustafa Ali Alhamzi, Fawwaz An-Nashef, Jameel Ahmed Elayah, Noman AL-Sayadi

item.title: Towards Unbiased On-Policy Distillation for Block Diffusion Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.05373v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: On-policy distillation (OPD) has emerged as an effective post-training paradigm for language models, with recent efforts extending it to block diffusion language models (BDLMs). However, existing studies focus almost exclusively on small block sizes, leaving distillation into student models with larger blocks underexplored. In this work, we investigate this regime and reveal two critical optimization biases that induce severe training instability. First, mismatched block boundaries between teacher and student cause \textbf{\textit{context misalignment}}, providing distorted supervisory signals that misguide student decoding. Second, even under aligned contexts, an \textbf{\textit{intrinsic optimization bias}} in OPD, where the student tends to rapidly absorb high-support signals while lagging on low-support updates, drives a premature confidence surge that traps weaker students in catastrophic overconfidence collapse. To resolve these, we propose \mbox{\textbf{Un-OPD}}, an unbiased on-policy distillation framework with two novelties for stabilizing BDLM training. First, Un-OPD introduces a boundary-aware step filtering strategy that eliminates context-misaligned decoding steps. Second, Un-OPD proposes moderating optimization intensity at high-support positions via a support-rebalanced confidence calibration, thereby bypassing overconfidence collapse. Beyond stability, we also introduce a rollout reuse mechanism to reduce rollout generation overhead. Extensive experiments on math reasoning and code generation benchmarks show that Un-OPD consistently stabilizes training and delivers superior performance while reducing wall-clock training time by approximately half.
item.dc:creator: Zaiquan Yang, Fei Wei, Yong Wang, Yudong Han, Yiyu Li, Zhuofan Zong, Gerhard Petrus Hancke, Xiangxiang Chu, Rynson WH Lau

item.title: Calibrated Evidence Inference With a Small, Permissively Licensed Open Model
item.description: arXiv:2610.07019v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Systematic reviewers who use a model to read randomized trials need each answer and a measure of how far to trust it. If the model is calibrated, so that its stated probabilities match how often it is right, a reviewer can accept its confident answers and check the rest by hand. This paper fine-tunes Qwen3-4B-Base with low-rank adapters and a classification head for evidence inference (Lehman et al., 2019; DeYoung et al., 2020): given a trial's article and a prompt that names an intervention, a comparator and an outcome, classify the result as a significant increase, a significant decrease or no significant difference. The articles of Evidence Inference 2.0 come from the open-access subset of PubMed Central, which includes articles under non-commercial and no-derivatives licenses, so the released model was fine-tuned only on the 1,431 of 2,657 training articles under CC BY, CC0 or the public domain; it is released under the Apache License 2.0 and runs on a laptop. On the test split, its expected calibration error is 0.017 and its log loss is lower than that of Gemma 4 31B-it given the same input zero-shot, meeting criteria registered on the Open Science Framework before testing. Its macro-F1, 0.925, is above every published result on that split that I found, though those systems used other inputs, scoring rules and prompt filters, and the test labels are public. Accepting its 80 percent most confident answers leaves an error rate of 2.6 percent among them. Context ablations show that the answers depend on the article, but the title alone carries some signal, which an informative title or recall of the trial could explain.
item.dc:creator: Johann Emmanuel Li

item.title: AdaptEvo: Learning under Imperfect Supervision through Confidence-Adaptive Training with Knowledge Evolution
item.description: arXiv:2610.11354v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rule-governed contextual decision tasks require models to apply specified rules to case-specific context and evidence. Written rules can leave gaps in decision guidance and process evaluation, while reference judgments vary in their support from the rules and evidence. To address these challenges, we introduce AdaptEvo, a framework for learning under imperfect supervision that couples confidence-adaptive policy optimization with evolving decision knowledge and evaluation rubrics. Its Training module uses Confidence-Adaptive GRPO (CA-GRPO) to balance outcome and process rewards according to reference confidence. Its Evolution module synthesizes reusable decision knowledge from recurring failures across training cases and refines process rubrics to detect overlooked errors. To support empirical evaluation, we construct an industrial multimodal content moderation dataset comprising a training set and In-Period and Out-of-Period test sets, with the latter collected under changed rules. Using Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, AdaptEvo achieves 61.9% exact-label accuracy and 72.2% binary decision accuracy on In-Period, exceeding GRPO by 7.5 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively. On Out-of-Period, the policy trained with CA-GRPO retains exact-label accuracy gains over the base model across evaluated checkpoints without injected decision knowledge, while GRPO declines with continued training. CA-GRPO also outperforms the tested fixed reward mixtures on both Out-of-Period metrics.
item.dc:creator: AllSpark Team

item.title: Neither True nor False: Do LLMs Represent Truth-Value Gaps in Plural Predication?
item.description: arXiv:2610.14438v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used to summarize and verify claims in critical sources that inform consequential decisions. Such claims are full of plural definites. If three of five patients improved after taking drug A, the claim the patients improved after drug A is not true, since two did not, yet its negation, the patients didn't improve after drug A, is not true either, since three did. In formal semantics, this truth-value gap is known as the Homogeneity Gap: both the plural definite and its negation are neither true nor false when the property holds for only a fraction of the plural referent. A model that cannot represent this gap turns mixed evidence into a clean verdict, an error that can be costly in high-stakes use. We introduce HomogeneityNLI, a diagnostic dataset of 1,000 minimal pair items crossing determiner, polarity, and group composition across ten logical conditions. Evaluating seven open-weight models, we uncover a pervasive Bivalence Bias: models assign plural definites their homogeneous truth conditions. In the zero-shot setting, no model recognizes the gap for both polarities in more than 15% of scenarios, and negated definites are judged False in 84% of cases. Explicit linguistic rules, chain-of-thought, and enumeration prompts produce unstable, model-specific effects that often entrench the bias. Our findings indicate that current open-weight LLMs acquire the truth conditions of plural predication but not its trivalent logic, and cannot yet be trusted to summarize or verify claims whose evidence is mixed.
item.dc:creator: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Yiping Li, Sachin Giri, Wan Du

item.title: Where Is the "Self" of a Large Language Model? -- From Self-Index to Self-Reference
item.description: arXiv:2610.16717v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Does a large language model have a self, and if so, of what kind? We separate two functional levels familiar from biology: a self-index, which distinguishes one's own material from external material and shapes processing, as corollary discharge does in nearly all animals, and self-reference, the higher ability to recognize what is one's own, as in mirror self-recognition. We probe both in Qwen3.8-27B by placing the same text in an Assistant, a User, or a System message rendered by the model's own chat template, and report three levels of evidence. Persistence: as predicted in advance, the representation of the text separates the model's own message from both external sources at all 64 layers and for every test text, along a shared direction, even when the answer does not depend on who supplied the text. Coupling: asked who wrote the preceding message, the model claims its own messages (0.77) and assigns User and System messages alike to the user, and how strongly it claims each message is predicted by the size of its self-index (Spearman correlation up to 0.68). Intervention: exchanging the internal states that follow a message, rather than those of its text, reverses the self-attribution between layers 15 and 31; removing the self-index direction from them at layer 39 lowers the claim more than a random direction; and in arithmetic the model adopts a wrong step more often when it wrote the step itself (0.92 versus 0.75), an effect carried by the step's representation at layers 31 to 39. Reasoning first in thinking mode raises the probability of the correct answer (0.96 instead of 0.77), but recognition is present without it. We propose that self-reference is a higher-level ability built on a self-index, a content-independent displacement superimposed on the whole representation of the model's own messages.
item.dc:creator: Yuchen Li, Xintong Li, Zongqi Fan, Ken-tye Yong, Nguyen H. Tran

item.title: A Bethe-Ansatz Source of Early Token Correlations: A marginal-preserving construction for parallel proposals
item.description: arXiv:2610.16781v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Parallel token proposals need a joint law, not merely accurate token marginals. We construct coordinate-Bethe-ansatz laws from the periodic XXZ chain and compare them with their maximum-entropy pairwise projections at identical one- and two-site moments. In an eight-site, three-excitation sector, symmetry makes the full probability-law difference one-dimensional, determined by a contiguous three-site moment $\delta$. Along the Bethe branch, this gap changes sign and vanishes exactly at $\Delta=(3+\sqrt3)/2$, where the eigenstate law becomes pairwise. A nonlinear two-token readout preserves separate token marginals yet exposes a distance $2|\delta|$; a direct three-token readout preserves all one- and two-token marginals yet exposes $4|\delta|$. At $\Delta=1.5$ these deterministic binary distances are $0.02654573$ and $0.05309145$. We give an exact target-alignment formula and prove a strict speculative accepted-prefix advantage throughout an unrestricted open neighborhood of a constructed target. These are finite-law existence results, not measured language-model or wall-clock gains.
item.dc:creator: Abraham Chachamovits

item.title: Knowledge Graphs as Files: An Agent Harness Where Tool Creation and Tool Use Co-Evolve
item.description: arXiv:2610.18616v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Searching text-rich knowledge graphs requires following relations while examining textual evidence. Predefined graph interfaces constrain what evidence agents can access, even when they write code to combine tool calls or process retrieved subgraphs. We propose direct knowledge graph interaction (DKGI), a harness in which language model agents create graph access tools directly over complete node and edge files. The agent writes Python code to follow relations, combine node sets, and select textual evidence, interleaving execution with shell search and file inspection. This lets agents process large node sets in bulk while returning selected text for the model to assess. Execution feedback guides tool creation and revision, while the evolving tools determine what evidence the agent gathers next. On benchmark datasets spanning three domains, training-free DKGI exceeds the strongest published baseline by at least 6.7 Hit@1 points on every graph, even with a minimal harness. Controlled ablations show the benefits of multi-turn programming over shell-only access and predefined graph tools, while trajectories show agents revising code to extend searches or address errors. These findings highlight the value of allowing tool creation and tool use to co-evolve during graph search. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/leopoldwhite/DKGI.
item.dc:creator: Yuyang Bai, Yu Wang, Yu Zhang

item.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
item.description: arXiv:2610.18726v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of $0.798$ across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with $0.776$ for a CNN and $0.751$ for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora.
item.dc:creator: Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter

item.title: Where Do LLM Ensemble Gains Come From? Decomposing Candidate Value, Diversity, and Aggregation
item.description: arXiv:2610.18786v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM ensemble gains are often measured against a single baseline, but the value attributed to additional candidates can change with the comparison used. We study an LLM aggregator under four matched conditions: Direct (no candidates), Single-slot (one candidate in a multi-slot interface), Duplicate (one candidate repeated), and Multi-candidate (separately generated candidates). Under either non-diverse control, overall candidate gain (CIV) splits algebraically into an additional-candidate contrast (DSV) and a candidate-context contrast (CCV); the split, but not CIV, depends on the chosen control. On MultiHopRAG model diversity (k=2), the repetition gap Rep=-8.33 pp [-13.25, -3.75] quantifies the difference between gains measured against Duplicate and Single-slot. On a matched FRAMES stronger-panel extension (n=200, k=3, aggregator output limit 4096), paired Delta Rep=+9.67 pp [+6.00, +13.50]; within panels, Rep changes sign (original -6.33; stronger +3.33). In FRAMES evidence aggregation, candidate-context contrasts remain strongly negative under both non-diverse controls. Our results show why ensemble evaluations should state the reference control before attributing gains to additional candidates.
item.dc:creator: Donghwan Kim

item.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
item.description: arXiv:2610.19705v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.
item.dc:creator: Xiaohan Wang, Haozhen Zhang, Qingyuan Liu, Tao Feng, Wenya Wang

item.title: JetSpec++: Foresight Parallel Drafting with Self Refinements
item.description: arXiv:2610.19792v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Speculative decoding's effectiveness is governed by two quantities: the acceptance rate of drafted tokens and the cost of producing them. We show the two objectives can be co-optimized with algorithm-system co-design, and present JetSpec++, which retains a strong learned draft model while hiding its cost almost entirely. JetSpec++ combines three components: intra-block self refinement, which trains the draft model to iteratively correct its own parallel predictions within a block of tokens; inter-block foresight drafting, which begins the next block before the current one is verified; and pipelined drafting and verification, which overlaps the two stages so drafting's marginal wall-clock cost approaches zero. In comparison with state-of-the-art speculative decoding methods, JetSpec++ attains a wall-clock speedup of up to $7.45\times$ over autoregressive (AR) decoding and $1.54\times$ over DSpark, with up to 1,361 tokens per second for a single request on GB200, and an average acceptance length of 8.94 across seven benchmarks, while preserving the target model's output distribution. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/hao-ai-lab/JetSpec.
item.dc:creator: Zhaoxiang Feng, Lanxiang Hu, Haoran Yuan, Yu-Yang Qian, Jihui Yang, Peng Zhao, Yibo Zhu, Tajana Rosing, Hao Zhang

item.title: Scaling Multilingual Mixture-of-Experts: How Language Coverage Changes Capacity and Compute Allocation
item.description: arXiv:2610.20247v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Multilingual models share capacity across languages, so adding languages can hurt performance on existing ones. Mixture-of-experts models expand this capacity with little additional per-token computation. Given this extra capacity, does adding experts reduce what each additional language costs? To answer this question, we propose a repetition-aware joint scaling law relating number of active parameters, training tokens per language, number of experts, and language coverage. Fitted on 26,300 per-language loss observations from 64 pretrained configurations, our law reduces prediction error on held-out configurations by 28% relative to the strongest evaluated baseline. At matched number of active parameters and training tokens per language, 32 experts reduce the loss penalty of expanding from 12 to 200 languages by 83% compared with a dense model. Our law further shows that broader language coverage favors more experts across a wider range of compute budgets, guiding capacity allocation as multilingual models scale.
item.dc:creator: Joel Dag, Nikit Srivastava, Hamada M. Zahera, Axel-Cyrille Ngonga Ngomo

item.title: Anuvani-Diarization: Zero Shot Speaker Diarization and Annotation Conventions Across 22 Languages
item.description: arXiv:2610.20327v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: India's 22 scheduled languages are spoken by over a billion people in conversations that mix languages, often within one turn, overlap freely, and take place over telephones, in meetings, and in media. Knowing who spoke when, the task of speaker diarization, is essential to speech applications for such conversation: voice agents conversing with several people at once, speaker attributed transcription of meetings and calls, contact center analytics, and media monitoring. We present a systematic study of speaker diarization across all 22 languages on IndicDiarBench and introduce Anuvani-Diarization, which adapts a self-supervised end-to-end segmentation model to Indian conversation with uncertainty aware silver supervision. Evaluated zero shot alongside nine recent diarization systems, it reaches a duration weighted diarization error rate (DER) of 16.78% on all 1,164 recordings, the lowest of all systems we ran and second only to the best published result (16.0%), and leads the three strongest rivals in 14 of 22 languages. It matches its parent on six international benchmarks. We also show that the benchmark's utterance level annotation convention is a hidden variable worth 1.9 to 4.1 DER points, depending on the system, and that a convention learned from other Indian transcriptions does not transfer.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Fernandes, Narayan Choudhary

item.title: Analyzing performance of Retrieval Augmented Generation models for Question Answering Tasks
item.description: arXiv:2610.20419v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have become almost a cornerstone of open-domain question answering tasks; in which the quality of answers generated in the process, greatly relies on the effectiveness of retrieval mechanisms.
